items.readable_text:
Content:
In this topic, we will consider a few more properties of determinants. Let's start with the following important property.

Content:
> The determinant of the product of two square matrices is equal to the product of the determinants.

Content:
Symbolically, if [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are both square matrices, then

Content:
[MATH: \det(A \cdot B) = \det(A) \cdot \det(B).]

Content:
For instance, suppose that we want to find the determinant of the matrix [MATH: A] that is defined as follows:
[MATH: [1|0|0; − 2|− 3|0; 2|0|2]]

Content:
To easily compute [MATH: \det(A)], we first compute the determinants of the two matrices and then multiply the results. Also, notice that both matrices in our product are triangular, so their determinants are given by the product of the diagonal entries:

Content:
[MATH: det(A)|= det[1|0|0; − 2|− 3|0; 2|0|2] ⋅ det[3|− 10|sqrt(2); 0|5|2sqrt(3); 0|0|− 1]; =|1|0|0; − 2|− 3|0; 2|0|2|_(⏟)_(lower triangular) ⋅|3|− 10|sqrt(2); 0|5|2sqrt(3); 0|0|− 1|_(⏟)_(upper triangular); = (1 ⋅ (− 3) ⋅ 2) ⋅ (3 ⋅ 5 ⋅ (− 1)); = (− 6) ⋅ (− 15); = 90]

items.title: Calculating the Determinant of a Product

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: [1|2|11; 0|− sqrt(3)|3; 0|0|3sqrt(3)]] find [MATH: \det(A).]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: [1|2|11; 0|− sqrt(3)|3; 0|0|3sqrt(3)]] find [MATH: \det(A).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Given two [MATH: n\times n] matrices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] we have

[MATH: \det(AB) = \det(A)\cdot \det(B).]

In our case, this gives

[MATH: det(A)|= det[1|2|11; 0|− sqrt(3)|3; 0|0|3sqrt(3)] ⋅ det[− 2|1|− sqrt(11); 0|5|− 1; 0|4|− 1].]

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

  • For the first determinant, we notice that it's upper triangular. Therefore, the determinant is simply the product of the diagonal entries.

  • For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the [MATH: 1]st column.

Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: det(A)|=|1|2|11; 0|− sqrt(3)|3; 0|0|3sqrt(3)|⋅|− 2|1|− sqrt(11); 0|5|− 1; 0|4|− 1|; = (1 ⋅ (− sqrt(3)) ⋅ 3sqrt(3)) ⋅ (− 2(− 1)^{1 + 1}|5|− 1; 4|− 1|); = (− 9) ⋅ ((− 2) ⋅ (− 5 + 4)); = (− 9) ⋅ 2; = − 18.]

Content:
One final important property of the determinant is that it is a linear in each row and column. For rows, for example, this means

Content:
[MATH: det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; ◻_{1} + △_{1}|◻_{2} + △_{2}|…|◻_{n} + △_{n}; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮]; = det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; ◻_{1}|◻_{2}|…|◻_{n}; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮] + det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; △_{1}|△_{2}|…|△_{n}; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮].]

Content:
For instance, it's easy to check that

Content:
[MATH: det[1|2; 3|4]^(⏞)^(− 2)|= det[1|2; 0 + 3|4 + 0]; = det[1|2; 0|4]_(⏟)_(4) + det[1|2; 3|0]_(⏟)_(− 6).]

Content:
Note that this property also holds for columns:

Content:
[MATH: det[⋯|◻_{1} + △_{1}|⋯; ⋯|◻_{2} + △_{2}|⋯; ⋮|⋮|⋮; ⋯|◻_{n} + △_{n}|⋯] = det[⋯|◻_{1}|⋯; ⋯|◻_{2}|⋯; ⋮|⋮|⋮; ⋯|◻_{n}|⋯] + det[⋯|△_{1}|⋯; ⋯|△_{2}|⋯; ⋮|⋮|⋮; ⋯|△_{n}|⋯]]

Content:
For example, we have that

Content:
[MATH: det[1|2; 3|4]^(⏞)^(− 2)|= det[1 + 0|2; 0 + 3|4]; = det[1|2; 0|4]_(⏟)_(4) + det[0|2; 3|4]_(⏟)_(− 6).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this topic, we will consider a few more properties of determinants. Let's start with the following important property.

Content:
> The determinant of the product of two square matrices is equal to the product of the determinants.

Content:
Symbolically, if [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are both square matrices, then

Content:
[MATH: \det(A \cdot B) = \det(A) \cdot \det(B).]

Content:
For instance, suppose that we want to find the determinant of the matrix [MATH: A] that is defined as follows:
[MATH: [1|0|0; − 2|− 3|0; 2|0|2]]

Content:
To easily compute [MATH: \det(A)], we first compute the determinants of the two matrices and then multiply the results. Also, notice that both matrices in our product are triangular, so their determinants are given by the product of the diagonal entries:

Content:
[MATH: det(A)|= det[1|0|0; − 2|− 3|0; 2|0|2] ⋅ det[3|− 10|sqrt(2); 0|5|2sqrt(3); 0|0|− 1]; =|1|0|0; − 2|− 3|0; 2|0|2|_(⏟)_(lower triangular) ⋅|3|− 10|sqrt(2); 0|5|2sqrt(3); 0|0|− 1|_(⏟)_(upper triangular); = (1 ⋅ (− 3) ⋅ 2) ⋅ (3 ⋅ 5 ⋅ (− 1)); = (− 6) ⋅ (− 15); = 90]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Determinant of a Product

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: [1|2|11; 0|− sqrt(3)|3; 0|0|3sqrt(3)]] find [MATH: \det(A).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given two [MATH: n\times n] matrices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] we have

[MATH: \det(AB) = \det(A)\cdot \det(B).]

In our case, this gives

[MATH: det(A)|= det[1|2|11; 0|− sqrt(3)|3; 0|0|3sqrt(3)] ⋅ det[− 2|1|− sqrt(11); 0|5|− 1; 0|4|− 1].]

We can compute the required determinants as follows:

- For the first determinant, we notice that it's upper triangular. Therefore, the determinant is simply the product of the diagonal entries.
- For the second determinant, we can compute it using a Laplace expansion down the [MATH: 1]st column.

Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: det(A)|=|1|2|11; 0|− sqrt(3)|3; 0|0|3sqrt(3)|⋅|− 2|1|− sqrt(11); 0|5|− 1; 0|4|− 1|; = (1 ⋅ (− sqrt(3)) ⋅ 3sqrt(3)) ⋅ (− 2(− 1)^{1 + 1}|5|− 1; 4|− 1|); = (− 9) ⋅ ((− 2) ⋅ (− 5 + 4)); = (− 9) ⋅ 2; = − 18.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Determinant of an Inverse Matrix

Content:
Another useful property of determinants is that, for any invertible matrix [MATH: A,] we have
[MATH: \det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)}.]

Content:
To understand why the above property is true, remember that [MATH: A \cdot A^{-1} = I] for any invertible matrix [MATH: A.] So, we have

Content:
[MATH: A ⋅ A^{− 1}|= I; det(A ⋅ A^{− 1})|= det(I); det(A) ⋅ det(A^{− 1})|= 1; det(A^{− 1})|= (1)/(det(A)).]

Content:
Important: We can only apply the formula [MATH: \det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)}] if [MATH: A] is invertible, meaning that [MATH: \det(A) \neq 0.]

---

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given an invertible [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: A,] we have

[MATH: |A^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|A|}.]

First, we find [MATH: |A|] using a Laplace expansion across the [MATH: 3]rd row:

[MATH: |A||=|2|14|− 1; 7|− 6|− 6; 0|− 3|0|; = − 3(− 1)^{3 + 2}|2|− 1; 7|− 6|; = 3 ⋅ (− 12 + 7); = − 15]

Therefore, we obtain

[MATH: \det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{|A|} = -\dfrac{1}{15}.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Linearity of the Determinant

Content:
One final important property of the determinant is that it is a linear in each row and column. For rows, for example, this means

Content:
[MATH: det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; ◻_{1} + △_{1}|◻_{2} + △_{2}|…|◻_{n} + △_{n}; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮]; = det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; ◻_{1}|◻_{2}|…|◻_{n}; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮] + det[⋮|⋮|…|⋮; △_{1}|△_{2}|…|△_{n}; ⋮|⋮|…|⋮].]

Content:
For instance, it's easy to check that

Content:
[MATH: det[1|2; 3|4]^(⏞)^(− 2)|= det[1|2; 0 + 3|4 + 0]; = det[1|2; 0|4]_(⏟)_(4) + det[1|2; 3|0]_(⏟)_(− 6).]

Content:
Note that this property also holds for columns:

Content:
